paper_title: Dusting the Phantom: Gaussian Allocation for Fading Dynamic Content

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Dynamic Gaussian representations have made high-quality, real-time volumetric video increasingly practical, yet challenging motion can still break their reconstruction: small fast-moving objects may disappear, and fine textures in highly dynamic regions are often lost. In particular, simply training longer or using more Gaussians may still fail to recover small, fast-moving objects. We argue that the key bottleneck is not representational capacity itself, but where and when Gaussian primitives are allocated. Existing allocation strategies rely on current Gaussian locations and often overlook the spatiotemporal destinations of relocated Gaussians. To address these limitations, we introduce two complementary strategies. First, Seed Injection identifies under-reconstructed dynamic regions using temporal appearance changes and reconstruction errors, and initializes new Gaussians at geometrically plausible 3D locations through multi-view observations, independent of existing Gaussian locations. Second, Temporal Biased Relocation uses time-resolved optimization signals to guide the spatiotemporal placement of relocated Gaussians. Both strategies maintain a fixed Gaussian budget without modifying the underlying representation. Experiments across multiple dynamic-scene datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction quality, particularly in highly dynamic regions, recovering small, rapidly moving objects and fine-grained appearance details.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recent advances in 4D volumetric video promise to transform how we experience visual content: rather than watching events from fixed, recorded viewpoints, viewers can freely explore dynamic scenes as they unfold in space and time. From free-viewpoint sports replays (Chen et al., 2019; Dai et al., 2024) and immersive performances (Collet et al., 2015) to lifelike telepresence (Lawrence et al., 2021), such experiences require faithful reconstruction of both appearance and motion, together with interactive rendering. Recent advances in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) (Mildenhall et al., 2021) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023) have brought this vision closer to reality, providing powerful representations for high-quality novel-view synthesis that have been successfully extended to dynamic scenes. In particular, 3DGSs high-quality, real-time rendering makes it especially attractive for next-generation immersive media, driving growing interest in Gaussianbased 4D scene modeling. Many approaches have been developed to extend 3DGS to dynamic scenes, modeling temporal variations through deformation-based models (Yang et al., 2024b; Wu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024; Bae et al., 2024) or explicit spatiotemporal Gaussian representations (Yang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Liao et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026; Yeom et al., 2026). Despite substantial progress, challenging dynamic content still remains difficult to reconstruct, with small, rapidly moving objects sometimes entirely disappearing (Fig. 1a) and fine textures in highly dynamic regions often being poorly recovered (Fig. 1b). natural remedy is to train longer or increase the representational capacity by introducing more Gaussian primitives. While these strategies can improve reconstruction quality, they come at additional computational cost and do not necessarily resolve more severe failures, such as the disappearance of small, rapidly moving objects  (Fig. 6)  . This suggests that increasing capacity alone is insufficient, motivating us to examine how Gaussian primitives are allocated during optimization. We therefore study these failures through the lens of Gaussian allocation: whether sufficient Gaussian support is assigned to challenging dynamic regions, and whether that support is placed at the appropriate spatial locations and timestamps. Gaussian allocation is commonly adjusted through densification (Kerbl et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024) and relocation (Kheradmand et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; 2026; Yeom et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). Densification increases representation capacity by cloning or splitting existing primitives, whereas relocation recycles low-contribution Gaussians by moving them to regions that require additional support, often while maintaining fixed Gaussian budget. Both strategies rely on the current set of Gaussians to determine where Gaussians should be allocated. As result, they struggle to place Gaussians in regions that are already poorly represented, which often correspond to challenging dynamic content such as small or rapidly moving objects. An insufficient number of Gaussians can hinder the reconstruction of fine appearance details and may even cause these objects to disappear altogether. To address this issue, we introduce the Seed Injection scheme, which injects Gaussian primitives directly from observations rather than deriving them from existing primitives. Specifically, Seed Injection identifies poorly reconstructed dynamic regions by combining temporal intensity changes with reconstruction error across synchronized multi-view images, and lifts selected observations into geometrically plausible 3D locations. By providing new Gaussian support independently of the current primitive distribution, it enables the model to refine under-represented dynamic regions and recover content that would otherwise remain missing. Beyond allocating Gaussian capacity to under-represented regions, complementary challenge lies in determining when and where relocated Gaussians should be placed. For example, FreeTimeGS (Wang et al., 2025) focuses on selecting which Gaussians should receive additional capacity, while the temporal destination of the relocated capacity receives less consideration. In particular, relocation scores are typically aggregated across timestamps, discarding information about when strong optimization signals occur: high-scoring Gaussian may indicate where Gaussian capacity is needed, but provides little guidance about the particular timestamp at which that capacity is most useful. We therefore introduce Temporal Biased Relocation, which preserves time-resolved optimization signals and uses them to guide the spatiotemporal placement of relocated Gaussians along the trajectories of selected target Gaussians. By explicitly accounting for when reconstruction difficulty arises, our strategy allocates Gaussian capacity to timestamps where it is most needed, complementing the spatial allocation addressed by Seed Injection and improving reconstruction quality in both overall scenes and highly dynamic regions. 2 Together, Seed Injection and Temporal Biased Relocation address two aspects of Gaussian allocation: allocating additional capacity to under-represented regions and determining appropriate spatial and temporal destinations for relocated capacity, respectively. We apply both strategies to FreeTimeGS, our baseline, without modifying its underlying representation. Our contributions are as follows: (i) We introduce Seed Injection, which allocates additional Gaussian primitives to poorly reconstructed dynamic regions and enables the recovery of content with insufficient or missing Gaussian support. (ii) We propose Temporal Biased Relocation, which incorporates temporal optimization signals into the relocation destination, allowing Gaussian capacity to be placed at more appropriate times and spatial locations. (iii) Experiments across multiple dynamic-scene datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction quality in both overall scenes and highly dynamic regions, including the recovery of small, rapidly moving objects.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting. Building upon 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023), dynamic approaches track or deform Gaussian primitives over time (Luiten et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b; Wu et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024), with recent methods further modeling multi-frame motion dependencies (Huang et al., 2026). Deformation-based approaches, however, remain dependent on primitives established during canonicalization, making initially under-represented content difficult to recover through subsequent deformation. Explicit spatiotemporal approaches instead model temporal evolution through 4D primitives, interpolation, flexible lifespans, or continuous trajectories (Yang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024; Liao et al., 2026; Yeom et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). FreeTimeGS (Wang et al., 2025), which serves as our baseline, introduces flexible temporal lifespans to model Gaussian appearance and motion over time. FreeTimeGS++(Lee et al., 2026) further improves initialization and optimization stability. However, these advances do not explicitly address how Gaussian capacity is allocated across space and time, leaving challenging dynamic regions potentially under-represented. SPIN-4DGS(Kim et al., 2026) addresses reconstruction under large inter-frame displacements by reducing cross-frame interference through attribute prediction from explicitly collected spatiotemporal positions. Our work instead targets Gaussian allocation as source of dynamic reconstruction failures, without modifying the underlying dynamic Gaussian representation. Gaussian Densification and Relocation. The original 3DGS adaptively clones or splits Gaussians based on positional gradients, while subsequent works improve density control through alternative densification criteria (Rota Bul`o et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026). Beyond densification, 3DGS-MCMC (Kheradmand et al., 2024) introduces relocation to redistribute underutilized Gaussian capacity. Dynamic methods additionally incorporate temporal properties such as lifespan, velocity, and visibility into density control (Liao et al., 2026; Sandu et al., 2026; Yeom et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). While these methods use temporal cues to guide primitive selection, the spatiotemporal destination of Gaussian capacity receives less consideration. Our method instead introduces new support in under-represented dynamic regions and uses timestamp-specific optimization signals to determine the temporal destination of relocated capacity. Gaussian Allocation for Under-Reconstructed Regions. Error-based densification (Rota Bul`o et al., 2024) directly targets under-reconstructed regions using reconstruction errors, but remains dependent on existing primitives as densification sources. LPM (Yang et al., 2025) alleviates this dependency by localizing error regions in 3D through cross-view feature correspondence, but relies on an external matching model, which may be less reliable in regions with weak visual correspondence. SpaceTimeGS (Li et al., 2024) enables guided sampling even in regions with sparse or missing Gaussian support, but still relies on the current Gaussian representation to provide coarse depth prior for localizing new primitives. In contrast, our approach directly lifts observations from underreconstructed dynamic regions into 3D using synchronized multi-view geometry, without relying on existing Gaussian support or an external correspondence model. 3 Figure 2: Overview of Seed Injection. We identify under-reconstructed dynamic regions from synchronized multi-view observations and sample candidate pixels from the resulting seed map. The sampled observations are lifted into 3D using multi-view geometry to initialize new Gaussian primitives independently of the existing Gaussian distribution. After optimization, the injected Gaussians provide additional support for dynamic content that is poorly represented or missing in the original reconstruction.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: In this section, we present our approach for improving Gaussian allocation in dynamic scene reconstruction through Seed Injection and Temporal Biased Relocation. We first review the FreeTimeGS representation and its Gaussian relocation strategy as preliminaries in Sec. 3.1. Then, Sec. 3.2 describes how the Seed Injection technique introduces Gaussian primitives into under-reconstructed dynamic regions, and Sec. 3.3 details how Temporal Biased Relocation redistributes Gaussian capacity across time based on temporal optimization signals. 3.1 PRELIMINARIES FreeTimeGS representation. FreeTimeGS (Wang et al., 2025) represents dynamic scene using Gaussian primitives that can appear at arbitrary spatial locations and timestamps. Each Gaussian includes spatial position µx, temporal center µt, duration d, velocity v, and opacity σ, along with standard 3DGS attributes. To model local motion, FreeTimeGS assigns each Gaussian linear motion function, µx(t) = µx + v(t µt), (1) where µx(t) denotes the spatial position of the Gaussian at timestamp t. The contribution of each Gaussian over time is further controlled by temporal opacity function, (cid:32) σ(t) = exp (cid:18) µt 1 2 (cid:19)2(cid:33) . (2) The final opacity is obtained by multiplying the base opacity by σ(t), where µt and control the temporal center and extent, respectively. FreeTimeGS relocation. FreeTimeGS maintains fixed Gaussian budget by periodically recycling low-opacity Gaussians through relocation. Specifically, it defines sampling score for each Gaussian primitive as = λgg + λoσ, (3) where and σ denote the spatial gradient and opacity of the Gaussian primitive, respectively, and λg and λo are their corresponding weights. At each relocation interval, Gaussian primitives whose opacity falls below predefined threshold are reused and relocated toward primitives with high sampling scores.

Consequently, highly dynamic regions, particularly those with insufficient Gaussian support, may have limited opportunities to receive additional capacity. To address this limitation, we introduce Seed Injection, which identifies underreconstructed dynamic regions from image observations and introduces new Gaussian primitives independently of the existing Gaussian distribution. Further implementation details are provided in the supplementary material A.2. 5 Gaussian Injection. For each lifted seed xseed, we reinitialize an available low-opacity Gaussian at the seed position, keeping the total Gaussian budget unchanged. The number of injected Gaussians is limited by both the retained seeds and the available low opacity primitives. Its scale is initialized isotropically based on the pixel footprint at the estimated depth, following prior works (Barron et al., 2021; Baranowski et al., 2026). Similar to the initialization strategy of FreeTimeGS (Wang et al., 2025), we initialize its velocity from the displacement to the nearest lifted seed in the subsequent frame. This nearest-neighbor displacement is used only as coarse motion initialization and does not assume temporal correspondence between the seeds. The injected Gaussians thus provide new optimization starting points in under-represented regions and are subsequently optimized jointly with the existing representation. Training Procedure. We begin Seed Injection at the midpoint of training, when reconstruction errors provide informative signals for identifying under-reconstructed regions. Before performing any injection, we compute and cache the lifted 3D seed candidates for all training frames using the same model snapshot. Since the injected Gaussians are introduced directly rather than through standard optimization, we allow them to adapt to the current scene representation before resuming relocation. We then temporarily disable relocation and process the training frames sequentially. For each frame, we initialize up to Nmax Gaussians at the cached seed locations by reinitializing available low-opacity primitives, followed by 10 optimization iterations on that frame. These framespecific iterations are included in the original total training budget. After all frames have been processed, we resume the original frame-sampling schedule while keeping relocation disabled for an additional 10Nframes iterations, where Nframes denotes the number of temporal frames in the training sequence. Relocation is then re-enabled according to the original schedule. 3.3 TEMPORAL BIASED RELOCATION As described in Sec. 3.1, FreeTimeGS (Wang et al., 2025) reuses Gaussians whose opacity falls below predefined threshold and relocates them toward primitives with high sampling scores. However, FreeTimeGS pays limited attention to when additional Gaussian capacity is needed, potentially leading to suboptimal temporal allocation. To address this limitation, we propose Temporal Biased Relocation, which preserves timestamp-specific positional gradients and uses them to determine the relocation time. We follow FreeTimeGS (Wang et al., 2025) for selecting both the Gaussian to be relocated and the target Gaussian. We interpret this as signal that the current Gaussian allocation provides insufficient support at that timestamp. We additionally adjust the temporal duration to account for the shifted temporal center, while the remaining parameters follow the original FreeTimeGS (Wang et al., 2025) relocation scheme. Further details of the duration adjustment and relocation procedure are provided in the supplementary material A.2.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Datasets. We evaluate our method on three datasets with varying levels of scene dynamics. For N3DV (Li et al., 2022), we use all six scenes, each containing 300 frames captured at 30 FPS with 1921 cameras at resolution of 2704 2028. We downsample the images by 2, use camera 0 for testing, and use the remaining cameras for training. For CMU Panoptic (Joo et al., 2015), we use six 150-frame sequences captured at 30 FPS and 640 360 resolution, with 27 cameras for training and cameras 0, 10, 15, and 30 for testing. Following the camera configuration, we set the near plane to 0.5 for test-view rendering to suppress artifacts from Gaussians located near the test cameras. Finally, we introduce the Custom dataset, consisting of the Baseball and Break sequences, to evaluate reconstruction of small and rapidly moving objects. Existing dynamic-scene datasets provide limited coverage of such challenging motions, despite small and fast-moving objects being particularly difficult to reconstruct with current 4DGS methods. We therefore captured two sequences specifically designed to include these cases using synchronized multi-camera setup. The Baseball and Break sequences contain 250 and 300 frames, respectively, at resolution of 1920 1080 and frame rate of 30 FPS. Both sequences are captured using 23 cameras, with one spatially intermediate camera reserved for testing. For evaluation on dynamic regions, we generate test-view masks using SAM3 (Carion et al., 2026), as ground-truth dynamic masks are unavailable. We use dataset-specific prompts to segment the moving objects and report masked metrics using the resulting masks. For extremely fast-moving objects that are not reliably captured by SAM3, we additionally incorporate the dynamic masks used for Seed Injection to ensure that these regions are included in the evaluation. Evaluation metrics include PSNR, dynamic masked PSNR, DSSIM (Wang et al., 2004), and LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018). All experiments use an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB), except RealTime4DGS (Yang et al., 2024a), which uses an NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB) for both training and evaluation. Implementation Details. We build on the reproduced FreeTimeGS (Wang et al., 2025) implementation and follow its default training configuration unless otherwise specified. We use 500K Gaussians for N3DV (Li et al., 2022) and CMU Panoptic (Joo et al., 2015), and 1.5M Gaussians for the Custom dataset. We train N3DV, CMU Panoptic, and the Custom dataset for 30K, 50K, and 100K iterations, respectively, with longer training for the Custom dataset due to its more challenging outdoor scenes and high-frequency background details. For Seed Injection, we select = 8 synchronized cameras to construct the dynamic error-based seed maps, with Nseed = 48 candidates sampled per view and maximum of Nmax = 256 injected seeds per frame. The velocity and scale are initialized as described in Sec. 3.2, while opacity and temporal duration are initialized to 0.05 and 0.03, respectively. Temporal Biased Relocation is applied whenever relocation is performed throughout training. Table 1: Quantitative comparison on the N3DV dataset. Quantitative comparisons are presented in Table 1, with additional qualitative results provided in Fig. 12. Our method improves reconstruction quality over the FreeTimeGS baseline, with particularly noticeable improvements in dynamic regions, while preserving the well-reconstructed static content. CMU Panoptic We further evaluate our method on CMU Panoptic (Joo et al., 2015), which contains diverse and highly dynamic human motions. In particular, the Juggle sequence includes small and rapidly moving objects, providing challenging scenario where the juggling balls can be poorly reconstructed or even disappear due to insufficient Gaussian support. As shown in Fig. 3, our method successfully recovers the juggling balls while also better preserving the details of the rapidly moving hands. Beyond these challenging regions, our method improves reconstruction across variety of dynamic content. It also better allocates Gaussians to under-reconstructed static regions, leading to improved overall reconstruction quality. These improvements are reflected in the quantitative results in Table 2. Additional qualitative results on the other CMU Panoptic sequences are provided in the supplementary material  (Fig. 13)  . Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on the CMU Panoptic Juggle sequence. Our method better reconstructs the rapidly moving juggling balls while preserving fine details of the hands. Custom Dataset We next evaluate our method on the Custom dataset, consisting of the Baseball and Break sequences. Quantitative results are reported in Table 3, with additional qualitative comparisons provided in the supplementary material. In the Baseball sequence, the rapidly moving ball and baseball bat disappear in the FreeTimeGS reconstruction, while fine details of the glove are poorly preserved. As shown in Fig. 1a, our method successfully recovers the missing baseball, demonstrating its effectiveness in reconstructing small and rapidly moving objects. Our method also better preserves the details of the bat and glove, as shown in Fig. 1b. Similarly, in the Break sequence, our method successfully reconstructs the small and rapidly moving pirate roulette that is missing in the baseline  (Fig. 14)

sections.title: 4.3 ABLATION STUDIES AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: Component Ablation. We conduct an ablation study on three highly dynamic CMU Panoptic (Joo et al., 2015) sequencesBasketball, Football, and Juggleand report the average results across the three sequences to evaluate the contribution of each proposed component. As shown in Table 4, Seed Injection helps recover rapidly moving objects, such as the juggling balls, that are poorly represented by the baseline, while Temporal Biased Relocation improves reconstruction quality across both dynamic and under-reconstructed static regions, as shown in Fig. 4. Combining both components further improves reconstruction quality while introducing only small increase in training time, with all CMU Panoptic experiments using 500K Gaussians and 50K training iterations. We further analyze the sensitivity of Seed Injection to its key design parameters, including Nseed, Nmax, and the number of camera views, in the supplementary material (A.3). sections.title: 5 CONCLUSIONS
sections.content: We presented Gaussian allocation framework for improving the reconstruction of challenging dynamic content in 4D Gaussian Splatting. Our approach addresses two complementary limitations in existing allocation strategies. Seed Injection introduces new Gaussian primitives directly from synchronized multi-view observations, providing additional support for under-represented dynamic regions even when suitable Gaussians are absent from the current representation. Temporal Biased Relocation preserves time-resolved optimization signals to guide relocated Gaussian capacity toward the timestamps where it is most needed. We integrate both strategies into FreeTimeGS while preserving its underlying representation. Experiments across multiple dynamic-scene datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in reconstruction quality, particularly in highly dynamic regions, while recovering small and rapidly moving objects that can disappear in the baseline reconstruction. These results highlight the importance of explicitly considering both spatial and temporal Gaussian allocation for robust dynamic-scene reconstruction. Limitations. Our Seed Injection relies on simple frame-difference-based criterion to identify dynamic regions by comparing adjacent frames. Consequently, rapidly moving objects may not be detected when their appearance is similar to the surrounding regions, resulting in weak temporal differences despite substantial motion. In such cases, Seed Injection may fail to introduce additional Gaussian primitives into these under-reconstructed dynamic regions. We leave addressing this limitation to future work. In addition, although we evaluate our method on multiple dynamic-scene datasets, further evaluation on more diverse and highly dynamic datasets would be valuable as such datasets become available.

sections.title: A APPENDIX
sections.content: A.1 EFFECT OF INCREASED MODEL CAPACITY AND TRAINING We further investigate whether the missing dynamic content in FreeTimeGS can be recovered simply by increasing model capacity and training time. As shown in Fig. 6, even when both the number of Gaussians and training iterations are doubled, FreeTimeGS still fails to reconstruct the rapidly moving ball. In contrast, our method successfully recovers the ball using the original Gaussian budget and training schedule. This suggests that the failure is not merely caused by insufficient model capacity or optimization time, but by ineffective Gaussian allocation in challenging dynamic regions. Figure 6: Effect of increased Gaussian capacity and training iterations. Even with twice the number of Gaussians (3M) and training iterations (0.2M), FreeTimeGS fails to recover the rapidly moving ball, while our method successfully reconstructs it with 1.5M Gaussians and 0.1M iterations. A.2 ADDITIONAL IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS Figure 7: Construction of the dynamic error-based seed map. The reconstruction error map is computed from the difference between the ground-truth and rendered images, while the dynamic mask is obtained from the intersection of temporal difference masks from adjacent frames. The final seed map is obtained by element-wise multiplication of the reconstruction error map and the dynamic mask, highlighting under-reconstructed dynamic regions. Dynamic Error-based Seed Map. In this section, we describe the detailed construction of the seed map. As introduced in the main paper, the seed map is defined by combining reconstruction 14 error map with dynamic mask. As illustrated in Fig. 7, the construction consists of two main steps: computing the reconstruction error map and constructing the dynamic mask. The reconstruction error map is designed to capture regions that are insufficiently represented by the current Gaussian representation. Specifically, for each view at timestamp t, we compute the pixel-wise difference between the rendered image ˆIv,t and the ground-truth image Iv,t: (cid:13) (cid:13) (cid:13)Iv,t(p) ˆIv,t(p) (cid:13) (cid:13) (cid:13)1 Ev,t(p) = (10) , where denotes pixel coordinate. To restrict the reconstruction error to dynamic regions, we construct binary dynamic mask using the adjacent frames at timestamps 1 and + 1. We first convert Iv,t1, Iv,t, and Iv,t+1 into grayscale images and compute two temporal difference masks: v,t = 1 (cid:0)I gray rear v,t = 1 (cid:0)I gray front v,t gray v,t gray v,t1 > τ (cid:1) , v,t+1 > τ (cid:1) . (11) where τ denotes the intensity-difference threshold. We set τ =20 for grayscale intensities in [0,255]. The final dynamic mask is obtained by taking the intersection of the two difference masks: Dv,t = rear v,t front v,t . (12) This intersection retains pixels that consistently exhibit temporal changes with respect to both neighboring frames, while suppressing transient differences that appear only in one direction. Finally, we construct the seed map by multiplying the reconstruction error map with the dynamic mask: Mv,t(p) = Dv,t(p)Ev,t(p). (13) This allows the seed map to reflect the degree of under-representation measured by the reconstruction error, while restricting the response to temporally dynamic regions. Consequently, regions with large reconstruction errors in static areas are suppressed, whereas poorly reconstructed dynamic regions receive high seed values. Multi-view Seed Lifting. Alg. 1 describes the detailed process of Multi-view Seed Lifting. As mentioned earlier, we match seed candidates across views using the proximity of their viewing rays and use the resulting 3D locations to initialize new Gaussians. Algorithm 1 Multi-view Seed Lifting Require: Seed maps {Mv,t}, selected views St, candidates per view Nseed, maximum seeds Nmax Ensure: 3D seed positions Xseed 1: Sample Nseed seed pixels from each selected view and back-project them into viewing rays 2: Form all cross-view ray pairs 3: for each cross-view ray pair do 4: 5: 6: end for 7: For each ray, select its nearest valid partner, if any 8: Take the union of the selected ray pairs 9: Set each 3D seed to the midpoint of the corresponding closest points 10: Keep at most Nmax seeds with the smallest ray distances 11: return Xseed Compute the closest points and ray distance Retain pairs with positive depths and sufficiently close viewing rays Temporal Biased Relocation. Alg. 2 describes the detailed procedure of Temporal Biased Relocation. We follow the original FreeTimeGS strategy to select the Gaussian to be relocated and its target Gaussian, and determine the relocation timestamp using the target Gaussians timestampspecific mean 2D positional gradient magnitudes. 15 Algorithm 2 Temporal Biased Relocation Require: Gaussian set G, timestamp-wise mean 2D positional gradient magnitudes Ensure: Relocated Gaussians 1: Select the Gaussian to be relocated and the target Gaussian using the original FreeTimeGS relocation strategy Retrieve the mean 2D positional gradient magnitude associated with (g, t) 2: for each observed timestamp Tg do 3: 4: end for 5: Normalize the timestamp-specific mean gradient magnitudes over Tg to obtain Pg(t) 6: Sample the relocation timestamp Pg(t) 7: Set the relocated temporal center ˆµt 8: Set the relocated spatial center ˆµx µx + v(t µt) 9: Compute the targets temporal support radius 10: Set the relocated temporal duration ˆd min 11: Apply the remaining FreeTimeGS relocation updates 12: return relocated Gaussians ϵ, min{t(µtr), t(µt+r)} 2 ln 10 (cid:16) d, max 2 ln (cid:16) (cid:17)(cid:17) A.3 ADDITIONAL ABLATION STUDIES AND ANALYSIS Effect of the number of sampled seeds. We further investigate the effect of Nseed, which controls the number of seed candidates sampled from each camera view during Seed Injection. The primary effect of Seed Injection is to recover small and rapidly moving objects that may be completely missing in the baseline reconstruction and to improve fine details in fast-moving regions. Since these improvements are spatially localized to small regions and often persist for only short temporal duration, their impact may not be fully reflected in image-level quantitative metrics (e.g., PSNR). We therefore provide qualitative ablation with Nseed {4, 8, 16, 48} in Fig. 8. 16 Figure 8: Qualitative ablation on the number of sampled seeds Nseed on the Custom Baseball dataset. We compare different values of Nseed across three representative frames containing small Increasing Nseed leads to more consistent recovery of challenging and rapidly moving objects. dynamic content, including the baseball, bat, and glove. As shown in Fig. 8, the effect of Nseed varies depending on the frame and the dynamic content. At frame 17, the baseball glove is well reconstructed even with small number of injected seeds, whereas the baseball bat is barely visible with Nseed = 4 and 8. The bat begins to emerge at Nseed = 16, but its structure remains unclear, while Nseed = 48 produces more clearly visible reconstruction. At frame 92, in contrast, the rapidly moving baseball is successfully reconstructed across all tested values of Nseed. At frame 97, the baseball is completely missing with Nseed = 4, but becomes clearly visible from Nseed = 8 onward. Overall, these results show that the number of seeds required for successful reconstruction can vary across frames and dynamic content. While Nseed = 16 is generally sufficient to recover the target objects, we use Nseed = 48 in our main experiments to ensure more robust and stable seed generation across different frames and scenes. Effect of the maximum number of injected Gaussians. While Nseed controls the number of seed candidates sampled from each camera view, Nmax determines how many of the resulting 3D seeds are ultimately retained for Gaussian injection per timestep. We therefore investigate how sensitive the reconstruction is to the final number of injected Gaussians. As shown in Fig. 9, the reconstruction remains largely consistent across Nmax {16, 32, 64, 256}. Even with Nmax = 16, 17 challenging dynamic content, including the rapidly moving baseball, glove, and bat, is successfully reconstructed. This suggests that reconstruction quality is relatively insensitive to the final number of injected Gaussians once sufficient pool of seed candidates is available. Figure 9: Qualitative ablation on the maximum number of Gaussians injected per frame, Nmax, on the Custom Baseball dataset. We compare Nmax {16, 32, 64, 256} across three frames. Even with Nmax = 16, challenging dynamic content, including the rapidly moving baseball, glove, and bat, is successfully reconstructed. Effect of the number of camera views. Given the importance of having sufficient candidate rays for reliable seed construction, we additionally study the effect of the number of camera views used for multi-view seed generation. Fig. 10 shows qualitative results for {2, 4, 8}. With only two camera views, the limited set of cross-view ray candidates can lead to less reliable seed generation, resulting in inaccurate reconstruction of the rapidly moving baseball. In contrast, using four or more views successfully recovers the baseball, with similar reconstruction quality for = 4 and = 8. These results suggest that our method does not require large number of camera views for effective seed generation, with = 4 already sufficient for this sequence. Nevertheless, we use = 8 throughout our main experiments to provide more reliable multi-view correspondences across different frames and scenes. 18 Figure 10: Qualitative ablation on the number of camera views used for multi-view seed generation on the Custom Baseball dataset frame 9. Using only two views results in inaccurate reconstruction of the rapidly moving baseball, whereas four or more views successfully recover the object with similar reconstruction quality. Analysis of Temporal Biased Relocation. We further analyze the behavior of Temporal Biased Relocation (TBR) by measuring the number of relocation operations during training. As shown in Fig. 11, TBR consistently requires fewer relocation operations than the original FTGS, indicating more effective Gaussian allocation during optimization. Figure 11: Number of relocation operations during training on the CMU Panoptic dataset. FTGS denotes FreeTimeGS and TBR denotes Temporal Biased Relocation. A.4 QUALITATIVE COMPARISONS We provide additional qualitative comparisons on the N3DV, CMU Panoptic, and Custom datasets. Specifically, we present the Flame Steak, Sear Steak, and Cook Spinach sequences from N3DV, the Football and Baseball sequences from CMU Panoptic, and the Break sequence from the Custom dataset. 19 Figure 12: Qualitative results on the N3DV dataset. 20 Figure 13: Qualitative results on the CMU Panoptic dataset. Figure 14: Qualitative results on the Custom dataset.
